# About TK Partners Certified Public Accountant

## Identity

TK Partners Certified Public Accountant is a regional CPA firm. Its tagline is "Expert Accounting Services for Your Business." The firm provides outsourced accounting, tax, and estate and trust services to individuals and businesses, including small businesses, wineries, agricultural operations, restaurants, and estates and trusts.

**Locations and contact**
- Walla Walla Office: 5 W. Alder, Suite 215, Walla Walla, WA 99362
- Moses Lake Office: 1000 South Pioneer Way, Moses Lake, WA 98837
- Phone: 509 529-0941
- Email: info@tkpartners.com
- Website: https://tkpartners.com
- Primary call to action: Contact us

**Geographic scope:** Regional, serving Eastern Washington and the surrounding area from the two offices above.

**Team:** The firm is led by Kristal Hassler, CPA (CEO & Partner) and Mike Lemm, CPA (Principal). Client Managers include Carrie Shelton, Ellen Camp, Cameron Lewis, Erin Denney, and Connor McCaw (all CPAs), plus Missy Collin. Anne Riney is Director of Operations. Kristine Huntsman is Firm Administrator, and Linnea Nygren is Client Experience Ambassador. A group of Client Accounting Specialists supports day-to-day client work. The firm describes its team as CPAs and client accounting specialists who coach clients with patience and empathy and work to improve every day.

**Core services**
- **Outsourced Accounting:** Virtual bookkeeper, payroll, and tax. It gives growing businesses timely, relevant financial information to support confident decisions.
- **Business & Personal Income Tax:** Tax preparation, tax planning, and year-round tax advice. Delivery is through a secure, paperless process with digital document upload and e-signing.
- **Estates & Trusts:** Estate and trust planning, business continuity planning, asset protection, estate tax mitigation, and fiduciary administration. The work is coordinated with clients' attorneys, financial managers, and bankers.
- **Business Foundation Services:** Entity type analysis and accounting system setup for new businesses.

**Values:** The firm's five core values are Excellence, Leadership, Drive, Friendship, and Flexibility. Its values statement describes leading with empathy and kindness, treating clients with the patience and guidance of a compassionate coach, working to alleviate clients' pain points, improving daily, valuing relationships with clients and each other, and adapting to clients' changing needs.

**Voice:** Warm, supportive, and professional, with a partnership-oriented tone, light wordplay, and plain-language explanations. The aspiration is a caring, encouraging coach who is still highly competent: approachable but expert, never stiff or salesy. Example: "We're not just here to file your numbers. We're in your corner all year long, translating the tax jargon and helping you make your next move with confidence."

## Positioning & Differentiation

**Positioning statement:** A supportive partner, not just an accountant, with industry specialization in wineries, agriculture, and restaurants.

**Who the firm serves:** Small business owners, winery owners, farmers, ranchers and agricultural businesses, restaurant owners, startups and established companies, trustees and estate administrators, and individuals and families needing tax and estate planning.

**What clients need:** Reliable bookkeeping and payroll without billing surprises, proactive year-round tax and planning advice, industry-specific accounting (wine, agriculture, restaurants), and plain-language guidance through estates and trusts.

**Differentiators**
- A supportive, caring partner approach rather than a once-a-year transactional relationship.
- A fixed monthly fee for bookkeeping, with no billing surprises.
- A secure digital tax process with document upload and e-signing.
- Year-round advisory support, including tax planning, rather than filing only at tax time.
- Industry-specific accounting for wineries, agriculture, and restaurants.
- Plain-language explanations of tax and financial jargon.
- Estate and trust expertise, shown in dedicated service pages and in-depth articles on topics such as basis tracking, gift tax safe harbor, living trust myths, and inheritance costs.

## Industries Served

### Wineries
Specialized outsourced accounting for winery owners, including inventory management, cost accounting, and alcohol regulation compliance.

- **Value proposition:** Accountants who understand winery inventory, cost accounting, and alcohol regulations, so owners can focus on the wine.
- **Pain points:** Tracking inventory and cost of goods across vintages; alcohol regulatory compliance and reporting; bookkeeping that doesn't fit seasonal cash flow.
- **Focus areas:** Alcohol regulation compliance; inventory management and cost accounting.
- **Typical triggers:** A compliance issue or audit scare, or growth (a new tasting room, more distribution) that outgrows the current bookkeeper.

### Agriculture
Outsourced accounting for farmers, ranchers, and agricultural businesses, including farm budgets, subsidies, grants, and asset depreciation.

- **Value proposition:** Outsourced accounting built around ag realities, covering budgets, grants, and depreciation, with year-round planning instead of a once-a-year tax filing.
- **Pain points:** Farm budgeting and unpredictable income; tracking subsidies and grants; asset depreciation and tax planning.
- **Focus areas:** Farm budgets; subsidies and grants; asset depreciation; farm tax planning.
- **Typical triggers:** A large equipment purchase, land or operation expansion, or a tax surprise at year-end.

### Restaurants
Outsourced accounting for restaurants, covering inventory, cost accounting, payroll, tax filings, and food service regulatory compliance.

- **Value proposition:** A fixed monthly fee for bookkeeping, payroll, and tax, so owners get accurate numbers without billing surprises.
- **Pain points:** Thin margins and food cost control; payroll and tip complexity; inventory tracking; food service regulatory and tax compliance.
- **Focus areas:** Inventory and cost accounting; payroll and tax filings; food service regulatory compliance.
- **Typical triggers:** Opening a new location or restaurant, falling behind on books or payroll, or unclear profitability.

### Businesses
Outsourced accounting for startups and established companies, including financial planning, tax compliance, and cost management.

- **Value proposition:** A supportive partner for setup, bookkeeping, tax, and planning year-round, not just at filing time.
- **Pain points:** No financial system or entity structure in place; tax compliance; cost management; no time for the books.
- **Focus areas:** Financial planning, tax compliance, and cost management; entity type analysis and accounting system setup through Business Foundation Services.
- **Typical triggers:** Starting a business, outgrowing spreadsheets, or needing an entity-type decision or financial planning.

### Estates & Trusts
Tax administration and accounting support for trustees and estate administrators.

- **Value proposition:** Patient, plain-language guidance through estate and trust tax administration, so trustees can fulfill their duties with confidence.
- **Pain points:** Unfamiliar fiduciary tax rules; basis tracking and gift tax questions; the administrative burden on trustees during a stressful time.
- **Typical triggers:** A death or trust funding that makes someone a trustee or administrator, or an estate plan that needs updating.

## Estate planning that starts with the tax picture

TK Partners is an estate planning CPA in Walla Walla that handles the tax and numbers side of your plan while your attorney handles the legal documents. We support estate and trust planning, business continuity, asset protection, estate tax mitigation, and fiduciary administration for individuals, families, and trustees across Eastern Washington.

If you are not sure where to start, you are in good company. Most families begin with one question, like "what happens to the farm?" or "do we need a trust?" We turn that into a plan you can follow. Here is what that includes:

- **Estate and trust planning:** the numbers behind your wishes, including support for revocable and irrevocable trust setup.
- **Business continuity planning:** keeping a family business running through a transition.
- **Asset protection:** structuring ownership so what you built stays protected.
- **Estate tax mitigation:** reducing what the IRS and Washington State can claim.
- **Fiduciary administration:** accounting and tax support for trustees and administrators.

Think of us as the part of your plan that keeps good intentions from turning into surprise bills.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## How can you protect and pass on what you have built?

Federal estate tax gets most of the headlines, but Washington has its own estate tax, and it starts at a much lower threshold. A family that owes nothing federally can still owe the state. Thresholds change, so we confirm the current numbers with you instead of quoting them from memory.

One point settles a common search: Washington has no inheritance tax. Beneficiaries do not pay a state tax simply for receiving an inheritance. They can still face income tax questions on things like retirement accounts or the sale of inherited property, which is why beneficiary tax planning matters.

Good estate tax planning usually comes down to four things:

- Estimating what your estate could owe at the federal and state level, then modeling ways to lower it.
- Choosing how assets are titled and held, which is the heart of asset protection.
- Tracking basis, the starting value used to calculate taxable gain, so heirs are not overtaxed later.
- Looking past the next generation, since multi-generational wealth planning means thinking about grandchildren, not just children.

Plans also go stale. A marriage, a divorce, a new grandchild, a death in the family, or the sale of a business can all change the math. If your plan was written before one of those, it is worth a second look.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: vineyard-family-succession-planning.jpg | alt: "Family owners walking through a vineyard row discussing the future of their winery" | query: "vineyard owners walking rows" -->
## Wineries, farms, and family businesses that need a succession plan

For a winery or a farm, the estate is rarely cash. It is land, equipment, barrels, and vintages sitting in inventory. When an owner passes away without a plan, heirs can be forced to sell part of the operation just to cover the tax bill. That is a hard way to learn what the estate was worth.

We work with winery owners and farm and ranch families across Eastern Washington on winery estate planning and agricultural estate planning. Business continuity planning and business succession planning are part of the same conversation: who runs it, who owns it, and how the tax works when the keys change hands.

The moments that usually start the conversation:

- A large equipment or land purchase.
- An expansion, like a new tasting room or more acres.
- An owner who is getting older and has not yet named a successor.

Erin Denney, CPA, our Tax Manager, brings entity structuring and multi-year tax strategy to closely-held and family-run businesses. Her work helps owner-operators choose how the business is held today, so the transfer tomorrow costs less. Already working with us on your books? We can pull your winery or ag numbers into the plan from day one. See how we support [wineries](/wineries) and [agriculture](/agriculture).

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: trustee-reviewing-estate-paperwork.jpg | alt: "Trustee sitting at a desk reviewing estate paperwork with a calculator and laptop" | query: "person reviewing estate paperwork desk" -->
## What do you do when you suddenly become a trustee or administrator?

One phone call, one funeral, or one signed trust, and suddenly you are the trustee. Nobody hands you a manual. You are now a fiduciary, which simply means you are legally responsible for managing someone else's assets with care. Fiduciary tax rules are unfamiliar, basis tracking is confusing, gift tax questions pop up, and it all lands during a difficult season.

We take the accounting and tax weight off your shoulders and explain each step in plain language. If a term needs defining, we define it. Here is what we handle for trust administration in Walla Walla, WA and across Eastern Washington:

- **Fiduciary accounting:** recording what comes in, what goes out, and what you owe beneficiaries.
- **Trust accounting:** clean, ongoing records for trusts that continue after a death.
- **Probate accounting:** the financial reports that go with the court process.
- **Estate settlement:** paying final bills and taxes, then closing things out properly.
- **Trust and estate tax return preparation:** including the fiduciary income tax return and any estate tax filings.

You do not have to figure this out alone. For a deeper look at the tax side, visit our [estate and trust tax administration](/estate-trust-tax-administration) page.

Families and trustees do not always live down the road. Our secure, paperless process lets you upload documents and e-sign from wherever you are, so a trustee in another state can stay fully involved. Estate work is scoped to your situation, and we talk through fees before we start.

### An initial conversation
We listen first. You tell us what is in the estate, what worries you, and what your attorney has already done.

### Coordination with your attorney
With your permission, we work directly with your estate attorney, so the legal documents and the tax plan fit together.

### Ongoing tax and accounting support
We keep the records, track basis, and prepare the returns, whether you need family trust administration in Washington or a one-time estate settlement.

### Year-round check-ins
We do not disappear after filing. Regular check-ins catch life changes and tax law shifts before they become problems.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: winery-barrel-room-tax.jpg | alt: "Oak wine barrels stacked in a winery cellar with a glass of red wine" | query: "winery barrel room" -->
## Winery tax planning that follows your vintages

Wine is not a one-year product, and your books shouldn't treat it like one. Inventory and cost of goods move across vintages, and a bookkeeper who doesn't track them leaves your tax return resting on guesses. Alcohol regulatory compliance and reporting add another layer, and the numbers you report there need to agree with the numbers on your return.

Owners often start looking for new help after a compliance issue or an audit scare. Others call when growth catches up with them: a new tasting room, wider distribution, a bookkeeper who has reached the edge of what they know. Both are good moments to start.

Winery tax planning in Walla Walla works best with accountants who understand winery inventory, cost accounting and alcohol regulations. That is the whole point of working with us. You focus on the wine, and we keep the [winery books](/wineries) and the return in step with each other.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: farm-field-equipment.jpg | alt: "Tractor working a wheat field at sunset in farmland" | query: "farmer tractor wheat field" -->
## How can farm and ranch tax preparation avoid a year-end surprise?

The worst tax news arrives in December or January, when nothing can be done about it. Farm income is unpredictable, so a strong year and a tax bill you didn't see coming often show up together.

Planning during the year changes that. We look at where income is running, then decide what to do about it while there is still time to act. That includes how subsidies and grants are tracked and reported, so they land in the right place on your return.

Depreciation is the other big lever. A large equipment purchase, new land, or an expansion of the operation all change your tax picture. Talk to us before you sign, and we can plan the depreciation around the purchase instead of reacting to it afterward.

If you need agricultural tax preparation or farm tax services in Walla Walla, our [agriculture team](/agriculture) builds the plan around ag realities: budgets, grants, depreciation and a calendar that follows the seasons.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: restaurant-owner-ledger.jpg | alt: "Restaurant owner reviewing paperwork at a table inside a busy dining room" | query: "restaurant owner reviewing paperwork" -->
## Restaurant tax services for thin margins and tip-heavy payroll

Restaurants run on thin margins, so a small error in food cost or payroll shows up fast. Tips make payroll more complicated, inventory is always moving, and food service tax compliance has its own rules. If your books are behind, your tax return inherits every gap.

Restaurant owners often reach out at a turning point. They are opening a new location, falling behind on books or payroll, or unsure whether the place is actually making money.

Our answer is a fixed monthly fee for bookkeeping, payroll and tax. Your return is built from books that stay current all year, and your bill never surprises you. Restaurant tax services in Walla Walla should give you accurate numbers you can use on a Tuesday, not just a form you file in the spring. See how we work with [restaurant owners](/restaurants).

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## How does year-round tax planning in Walla Walla work beyond filing season?

Tax questions don't keep a filing calendar, so ask yours whenever it comes up. Call us in the summer before a big purchase. Call us in the fall when a good year makes you nervous. Year-round advisory support is part of how TK Partners works, because the best tax decisions are made before the deadline.

Erin Denney, CPA, is our Tax Manager, and multi-year tax strategy for owner-operators is a focus of her work. Owners of closely held wineries, farms and restaurants often face the same questions: how the business should be structured, when to time income and expenses, and what a decision this year means for the next three. Erin helps owners map those answers out across several years instead of one return at a time.

Before a big purchase or an expansion, we review entity structure and timing together. That is CPA tax planning in Walla Walla built around your plans. It gives you tailored tax strategies that fit your operation, with professional tax planning for the owner and preparation for the whole household.

### Business foundation services
URL: /what-we-do/business-foundation-services

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Start with the structure your operation will grow into

A winery adds a tasting room and starts shipping through distributors. A rancher signs for another parcel and a piece of equipment that needs its own payment plan. A restaurateur opens a second location across town. Each owner is making a big move, and each move asks the same quiet question: is the business built to hold what comes next?

Business foundation services in Walla Walla at TK Partners answer it with two things: an entity type analysis and an accounting system setup. Our CPAs in the Walla Walla and Moses Lake offices sit down with you before anything is signed, explain the choices in plain language, and build a structure that fits how you earn money. You get a coach in your corner, not a form-filler. Think of it as pouring the concrete before you frame the house.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: entity-type-analysis-meeting.jpg | alt: "CPA explaining business structure options to two owners at a conference table" | query: "accountant explaining options to business owners" -->
## Choosing between an LLC, S corporation and C corporation

The right answer depends on your operation, which is why our entity type analysis starts with your numbers. We weigh four things: your tax exposure, how you will pay yourself as an owner, your personal liability, and what happens at a future sale or succession. Whether you are weighing an S-corp vs LLC question or looking at LLC formation in Walla Walla, the goal is the same: a business entity selection you will still be glad of in five years.

- **Winery:** Several owners, an alcohol license and inventory held in barrels and bottles across vintages. How profits are split and how the license is held both shape which entity fits.
- **Agriculture:** Family ownership, land and equipment depreciation. Structure decides how those assets are held and how they pass to the next generation.
- **Restaurant:** Owner pay, payroll and tip complexity. The entity you choose changes how you draw income and how payroll is set up.

A wrong choice is expensive to unwind, and it usually surfaces at the worst time, like a sale or a tax bill. Erin Denney, CPA, our Tax Manager, builds this work around entity structuring and multi-year tax strategy for owner-operators, so today's decision still makes sense in year five.

We advise on structure and tax impact. State filing and legal drafting steps are coordinated with your attorney.

<!-- block: feature-grid | variant: 3-col -->
## Books built around how your industry earns its money

An accounting system set up for a generic business will strain the first time a harvest comes in or a tip pool gets split. We build the chart of accounts and reporting around your industry from day one, so the first year-end holds no surprises.

### Winery business setup in Walla Walla
icon: ClipboardCheck

Inventory and cost of goods tracked across vintages, so you know what each bottle costs to make. Reporting is set up for alcohol regulatory compliance, which keeps an audit scare from becoming a scramble.

### Agriculture business formation in Walla Walla
icon: TrendingUp

Farm budgeting that makes room for unpredictable income. Grants and subsidies are tracked as they arrive, and asset depreciation is organized before the equipment invoice lands.

### Restaurant accounting setup in Walla Walla
icon: Receipt

Food cost and thin margins visible every month, not at year-end. Tips and payroll are configured correctly from the first shift, and inventory tracking is built into the system.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: fixed-monthly-fee-bookkeeping.jpg | alt: "Restaurant owner reviewing monthly bookkeeping reports on a laptop with an accountant" | query: "restaurant owner reviewing finances laptop" -->

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: tax-documents-checklist.jpg | alt: "Tax forms and a checklist laid out on a desk beside a laptop" | query: "tax paperwork checklist desk laptop" -->
## Tax documents to gather for your personal and business return

Gather these before we sit down together and your return moves faster. The right paperwork also makes year-round tax advice possible: we can spot a planning move in March instead of finding it in April. This list supports our [Business & Personal Income Tax](/what-we-do/income-tax) service, and a printable PDF version of this tax documentation checklist is available from our team on request.

- Personal income tax forms: W-2s from every employer, 1099s for interest, dividends, retirement and freelance income, and 1098s for mortgage interest or tuition
- Last year's filed return, so we can match carryovers and spot changes
- Business tax forms and records: a current profit and loss statement and balance sheet
- Payroll reports, including quarterly filings
- Asset purchase records with the date, cost and invoice
- **Form W-9** (Request for Taxpayer Identification Number and Certification): the form a contractor or vendor supplies so you can issue a 1099
- **Form 8821** (Tax Information Authorization): lets us view your IRS records without speaking for you
- **Form 2848** (Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative): lets us represent you before the IRS, such as answering a notice

### Track your tax refund status
URL: /resources/refund-tracker

<!-- block: process-steps | variant: vertical -->
## Check your federal refund status in three steps

Waiting on a refund tests everyone's patience, but you can at least swap "any day now" for an actual status. If you're asking where is my tax refund Walla Walla WA, the answer almost always lives on one IRS page. Washington has no state personal income tax, so the refund you're tracking is almost always federal.

### Gather three details
You need your Social Security number or ITIN, your filing status, and the exact refund amount on your return, in whole dollars. Keep your return open beside you.

### Enter them in the IRS tool
Open the [IRS Where's My Refund? tool](https://www.irs.gov/wheres-my-refund), the official way to check your federal tax refund status online. It works about 24 hours after you e-file, or about four weeks after you mail a paper return. Pick the tax year you filed, then enter your details.

### Read your status message
"Return Received" means the IRS has your return. "Refund Approved" means your amount is confirmed and a send date is being set. "Refund Sent" means it's on its way. For direct deposit, your bank may need a few extra days to post it. The tool updates once a day, usually overnight, so checking every hour won't change the answer.

<!-- block: content-table -->
## How long a tax refund takes to arrive

The IRS issues most e-filed refunds in under 21 days. Paper returns take longer, and direct deposit beats a mailed check because there's no mail time. Here is the estimated tax refund timeline by filing method:

| How you filed | How you get paid | Typical timing |
|---|---|---|
| E-filed | Direct deposit | Most refunds in under 21 days |
| E-filed | Mailed check | Same processing, plus mail time |
| Paper return | Direct deposit | Four weeks or longer |
| Paper return | Mailed check | Four weeks or longer, plus mail time |

A return flagged for review or correction can take longer than any of these.

**Amended returns run on their own clock.** They don't appear in the regular tool. Use the IRS [Where's My Amended Return?](https://www.irs.gov/filing/wheres-my-amended-return-1) tool, which usually shows a status about three weeks after you file Form 1040-X. Amended returns are reviewed by hand, and current IRS guidance says to allow up to 16 weeks.

The fastest route to a clean submission is a complete, e-filed return. Sending your documents through our secure digital upload and e-signing process helps get it there without missing pieces.

*This guidance applies to tax year 2024 returns, filed in 2025, so use it when you're checking 2024 tax refund status. Last reviewed: [insert date of final IRS check].*

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: tax-refund-paperwork-review.jpg | alt: "CPA and client reviewing a delayed tax refund notice together at a desk" | query: "accountant helping client tax paperwork" -->
## What to do when your refund is late or missing

A late refund is stressful, but it's rarely a verdict on your return. Most delays trace back to one of a few causes, and each has a next step. If you need Walla Walla CPA tax refund help, we deal with the IRS alongside you, with your authorization.

- **Identity verification hold.** The IRS mails a letter before releasing the refund. Follow the letter's instructions exactly. If you've responded and weeks pass with no movement, call us.
- **Math errors or an e-file rejection.** A rejected e-file never reaches "Return Received," so fix the error and resend. A math correction usually brings a notice and a delay. Send us the notice and we'll read it with you.
- **Direct deposit details that don't match.** If the bank rejects the deposit, the IRS typically mails a paper check instead. Confirm your account and routing numbers, and call us if the check hasn't arrived.
- **An offset against another debt.** Past-due federal or state debts can absorb part or all of a refund. You'll get a notice explaining where the money went. Bring it to us if the numbers don't add up.

IRS guidance says to call when it's been more than 21 days since you e-filed, more than six weeks since you mailed a paper return, or the tool tells you to. Call us first if you'd rather not wait on hold. A missing tax refund in Walla Walla is solvable, and you don't have to solve it alone.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Refunds for wineries, farms, and restaurants

A business refund can run on a different timeline from a personal one. If you file as an owner-operator on a Form 1040, the Where's My Refund? tool tracks it like any individual return. Entity returns are different: the IRS tool doesn't cover them, so we pull IRS transcripts or call the IRS with you to see where things stand. We can't promise amounts or dates, but we can tell you exactly where yours is.

### Wineries
icon: ClipboardCheck

Winery refunds often trace back to inventory and cost-of-goods timing across vintages. When costs land in a different year than expected, estimates can overshoot. We reconcile that before filing, then help with winery tax refund tracking afterward.

### Agriculture
icon: Wrench

A large equipment purchase plus depreciation can leave a farm with overpaid estimates. Farm tax refund questions in Walla Walla usually start here. Where the refund or credit shows up depends on how the return was filed.

### Restaurants
icon: Receipt

Overpaid estimates and payroll timing, like quarter-end deposits and tip reporting, can create an overpayment. The return decides whether it's refunded or applied to next year's estimates. For any restaurant business tax refund, we check which one happened.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: year-round-tax-planning.jpg | alt: "Accountant and winery owner reviewing tax planning documents together at a desk" | query: "accountant client reviewing tax planning" -->
## Plan ahead so next year's refund holds no surprises

A big refund isn't a prize, and a surprise bill isn't bad luck. Both usually mean withholding or estimated payments were off all year. For farm and winery owners, the surprise tends to land at year-end, after the equipment purchase or the big harvest is already done. For restaurant owners, unclear profitability turns estimates into guesses.

We adjust through the year instead of only at filing time. That works because the books stay current: our fixed monthly fee for bookkeeping means no billing surprises, and the numbers are fresh enough to plan from. Erin Denney, CPA, our Tax Manager, builds multi-year tax strategy for owner-operators, including entity structuring. Learn more about our [income tax services](/what-we-do/income-tax).

## How TK Partners protects your information

This policy covers two groups: visitors to the TK Partners website, and clients of our Walla Walla and Moses Lake, WA offices. If you knew us as TKCPA, you're in the right place. Same firm, new name.

This is the TK Partners accounting privacy policy, and we wrote it in plain language, not legalese. You trust us with bank records, payroll files and tax documents. You should be able to read what happens to them without hiring a lawyer to translate. No surprises in your bill, and none in how your information is handled.

Effective date: [EFFECTIVE DATE: LEGAL REVIEWER TO FILL IN]

Last updated: [LAST UPDATED DATE: LEGAL REVIEWER TO FILL IN]

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## What information we collect

We collect two kinds of information, and the first is much bigger than the second.

### What clients share for accounting, payroll and tax work

To do the work well, we need real records. Depending on what you hire us for, that can include:

- Identity details, such as your name, address, date of birth, Social Security number or EIN
- Bank statements, credit card activity, payroll records and prior tax returns
- Tax documents such as W-2s, 1099s and K-1s

The specifics depend on your business. [Winery](/wineries) clients send inventory and cost records across vintages. [Farm and ranch](/agriculture) clients send budgets and grant or subsidy paperwork, so agricultural accounting privacy matters from the first upload. [Restaurant](/restaurants) owners send payroll and tip records. Whatever your industry, this is sensitive material, and we treat it that way.

### What the website collects

When you use our site, we may receive:

- Contact form entries, including your name, email address, phone number and message
- Emails you send us directly
- Standard analytics and cookie data, such as pages visited, browser type and approximate location [CONFIRM WITH FIRM: analytics tools in use]

Client information security in accounting starts with collecting only what the job needs. We don't ask for more.

## Resources

### Why your payroll provider sets an early-December deadline for year-end changes
URL: /resources/why-your-payroll-provider-sets-an-early-december-deadline-fo

That email from your payroll provider lands right as harvest wraps up and the holiday tasting weekends begin. It says something like "year-end changes must be submitted by December 5," and it is easy to file under *later*. Please don't. The deadline is not there to make your life harder. It is there so your W-2s and 1099s come out right the first time, which means no corrections, no amended returns, and no January phone calls asking why your health insurance is on the wrong line.

This post walks through why the cutoff exists and the four items winery owners in Walla Walla miss most often. It ends with a checklist you can hand to whoever runs payroll.

## Why the deadline falls in early December

Payroll providers don't just cut checks. They also prepare your W-2s, your 1099-NECs, and your fourth-quarter and annual filings. Employee W-2s are due by January 31, and so are 1099-NECs for contractors. Providers serve thousands of employers who all want changes at once, so they set an internal cutoff weeks ahead.

After that cutoff, your last few paychecks of the year are already running through a locked process. A change submitted on December 22 may not reach the final payroll. It may need a manual adjustment, or it may only be fixable after the year closes, through a corrected W-2c. The IRS charges penalties for incorrect information returns, and they grow the longer a mistake sits. Fixing a problem before the books close is almost always cheaper and calmer than fixing it afterward.

If your provider's notice names a date, treat it as your real deadline. Your CPA's review should happen a few days before it, not after.

## Bonuses and harvest pay: the pay date decides the tax year

For employees, a bonus belongs to the year it is paid, not the year it was earned. Picture a cellar team of 12 who each earn a $1,500 harvest bonus, $18,000 in total. If that money goes out December 20, it lands on this year's W-2s. If it slips to January 3, it lands on next year's, and your employees' tax picture changes with it.

Three details are worth confirming before the cutoff:

- **Withholding method.** Bonuses are supplemental wages. Many employers withhold a flat 22 percent federal rate on them, but your provider needs to know which method you want.
- **Who is included.** Tasting room staff, seasonal crush crew, and anyone who left mid-season are easy to forget.
- **Owner pay.** If you are an S-corp owner, a year-end bonus to yourself interacts with your reasonable salary and your distributions. That is a planning conversation, not a last-minute payroll tweak.

That last point is where multi-year thinking pays off. Erin Denney, CPA, our Tax Manager, spends much of her time on entity structure and multi-year tax strategy for closely held, owner-operated businesses. Owner compensation is one of the first things she looks at. The best time to raise it is early December, while there is still a payroll left to act on.

## S-corp owner health insurance belongs on your W-2

This is the item we see missed most. If your winery is an S corporation and you own more than 2 percent of it, the IRS treats you as a "2% shareholder." Health insurance premiums the company pays for you must be included in your W-2 wages (Box 1). They are generally not subject to Social Security and Medicare tax, so Boxes 3 and 5 stay unchanged.

Here is what that looks like with real numbers. Say you pay yourself a $60,000 salary and the winery covers $1,800 a month in health premiums, or $21,600 for the year. Your Box 1 should show $81,600, while Boxes 3 and 5 still show $60,000. If payroll never hears about the premiums, Box 1 reads $60,000 and your personal return has nothing to support the self-employed health insurance deduction. That deduction is the reason for the whole exercise.

The fix is simple if it happens before the cutoff. Send your provider the year-to-date premium total and the monthly amount through December. Also confirm the company, not you personally, is paying or reimbursing the premiums. If you pay out of pocket with no reimbursement through the business, the setup doesn't work the way people assume. A short call with your CPA in November clears that up.

Spouses, children, and other family members on the payroll bring their own wrinkles. Mention them.

## Company vehicle use is a taxable fringe benefit

Winery owners and managers drive a lot: vineyard visits, distributor drop-offs, a Seattle trade tasting, a trip to the bank. When the business owns or leases the vehicle and someone also uses it personally, the personal portion is a taxable fringe benefit. That includes commuting. It must be added to that person's wages, and [IRS Publication 15-B](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-publication-15-b) explains the valuation methods.

The math is not scary, but it needs a record. If your vehicle qualifies for the cents-per-mile method, the 2025 IRS rate is 70 cents per mile. Say your general manager drove 3,000 personal miles in the winery truck. That adds $2,100 to taxable wages. Without a mileage log, you are guessing, and the IRS tends to assume the personal share is higher than you would.

To get it right, pull your odometer readings and your log by the first week of December and send the personal-use total to payroll. If you are weighing a new truck or SUV for next season, our post on [leasing versus buying a vehicle](/resources/auto-leasing-vs-buying-which-makes-more-sense) covers the cash flow and deduction side. Either way, the personal-use reporting question follows you.

## Employee data, contractors, and winery-specific perks

A W-2 is only as good as the data behind it. Names that don't match Social Security records, old mailing addresses, and missing Social Security numbers are the most common reasons returns bounce back or W-2s never reach the employee. Seasonal staff are the biggest risk. Someone who worked three weeks of crush in October may have moved twice since.

Before the cutoff, confirm:

- Legal names and Social Security numbers for everyone paid this year, including seasonal workers.
- Current mailing addresses, and whether each person has agreed to electronic W-2 delivery.
- A signed W-9 for every contractor, such as a vineyard management crew, a freelance bookkeeper, or a label designer, before you issue 1099-NECs.
- Tasting room tips, including card tips paid out through payroll, so reported tips match what lands on the W-2.
- Any wine allowance or staff case program. Employee discounts on your own products are excludable only within IRS limits, and free cases beyond those limits may be taxable wages. Check [Publication 15-B](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-publication-15-b) or ask us.

Washington has no state income tax, but your quarterly state filings still depend on correct wages and hours. Errors in year-end data can ripple into those reports too.

## A year-end payroll checklist for wineries

| Item | What to send payroll | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Bonuses | Amounts, recipients, pay date, withholding method | The pay date decides the tax year |
| S-corp owner health insurance | Year-to-date and December premium totals | Puts the premiums in Box 1 so the deduction is supported |
| Company vehicle | Personal-use miles or value per driver | Adds the taxable fringe benefit to wages |
| Wine perks and staff cases | Retail value and who received them | Prevents unreported taxable wages |
| Employee records | Names, SSNs, addresses, e-delivery consent | Avoids returned W-2s and mismatches |
| Contractors | W-9s and total paid | Needed to file 1099-NECs by January 31 |
| Final payroll date | Confirmation of the last run before December 31 | Keeps pay in the intended year |

The IRS also keeps plain-language pages on [employment taxes](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/employment-taxes) and [Form W-2](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-w-2) if you want to see how the boxes fit together.

If you offer a 401(k), December 1 matters too. Our post on [why 401(k) safe harbor decisions happen in November](/resources/safe-harbor-safe-timing-why-your-401-k-decisions-happen-in-n) explains that timeline, and it pairs well with this checklist.

## What a CPA review adds before the cutoff

Payroll software processes what you tell it. It can't tell you that your owner health insurance is missing, or that a bonus should wait until January. A short review a week before your provider's deadline catches those gaps while they are still cheap to fix.

Our clients on a fixed monthly fee for bookkeeping and payroll support get year-round advisory help, so this check is part of the rhythm and not an extra bill. Documents move through our secure digital process, so you are not emailing Social Security numbers or premium statements. If you want to see how we work with [Walla Walla wineries](/wineries), that page covers vintage-level cost accounting and compliance support.

## Common Questions

**What happens if I miss my payroll provider's year-end deadline?**

Your change may not reach the final payroll, so the error shows up on W-2s or 1099s. You would then file a corrected W-2c or amended return in January or later. Corrections cost time, and penalties for incorrect information returns increase the longer they stay uncorrected.

**Do S-corp owners really have to put health insurance on the W-2?**

Yes, if you own more than 2 percent. The premiums the company pays are reported in Box 1 wages, generally without Social Security and Medicare tax. That reporting is what supports your self-employed health insurance deduction on your personal return. Leaving it off can cost you the deduction.

**Is using the winery truck to commute taxable?**

Yes. Commuting and other personal use of a company vehicle count as a taxable fringe benefit. The value, often figured per mile, is added to wages. Keep a mileage log through December and send payroll the personal-use total before the provider's cutoff.

## Get your year-end payroll changes in early

If your provider's deadline notice is sitting in your inbox, send us the details now: bonuses, owner health premiums, vehicle miles, and any employee changes. We will review them with you and help you submit clean numbers before the cutoff. [Contact TK Partners](/contact) to set up a quick year-end payroll review.

### Safe harbor, safe timing: Why your 401(k) decisions happen in November
URL: /resources/safe-harbor-safe-timing-why-your-401-k-decisions-happen-in-n

Most winery owners in the Walla Walla Valley spend September and October with their eyes on the crush pad, not the plan document. Then Thanksgiving weekend fills the tasting room, December arrives, and someone remembers that the 401(k) has a notice deadline. For a calendar-year plan that uses a safe harbor match, the deadline is December 1. Missing it can turn a plan that skips annual testing into one that has to pass it, and that is when owners learn their own deferrals may be capped or refunded.

November is the month to fix that. This article covers what the deadline is, which safe harbor design suits a winery payroll, who has to receive the notice, and how the choice affects your tax return. It also covers what to do if you do not have a 401(k) yet.

## The December 1 deadline and who it applies to

A traditional safe harbor 401(k) trades a required employer contribution for relief from the annual nondiscrimination tests. In exchange, the employer must give every eligible employee a written notice before the plan year starts. The window is 30 to 90 days before the first day of the plan year. For a plan that runs January 1 through December 31, the last day to deliver it is around December 1, and the window opens in early October.

The notice explains the following:

- Which safe harbor contribution the employer will make
- How employees can defer, and the plan's rules on withdrawals and vesting
- When they can change their deferral election
- Where to find the plan's other details

The IRS describes the basic safe harbor structure in its [401(k) plan overview](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-sponsor/401k-plan-overview), and the broader [retirement plans pages](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans) are worth bookmarking for plan sponsors.

There is one wrinkle worth knowing. Since the SECURE Act, a plan that uses the 3% nonelective contribution no longer has to send the annual safe harbor notice at all. A plan using a matching contribution still does. So the December 1 date bites hardest for the matching designs, which are also the most common ones among small employers.

Timing also matters because a safe harbor design is generally a full-year commitment. Once the plan year starts, you cannot casually drop the contribution because a harvest came in light. That is why the decision belongs in November, when you can still pick a design you can afford.

## Which safe harbor design fits a winery payroll

There are four common choices. They differ in cost, predictability, and vesting.

| Design | Employer contribution | Vesting | Annual notice required? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Basic match | 100% of the first 3% of pay deferred, plus 50% of the next 2% (4% of pay maximum) | Immediate | Yes |
| Enhanced match | At least as generous as the basic match at every deferral level | Immediate | Yes |
| Nonelective | 3% of pay to every eligible employee, whether or not they defer | Immediate | No (since the SECURE Act) |
| QACA (automatic enrollment safe harbor) | Match of 100% of the first 1% plus 50% of the next 5%, or 3% nonelective | Up to 2 years | Yes for the match; no for the 3% nonelective |

Each one suits a different kind of winery.

### The match works when participation is uneven

Winery payrolls are lumpy. You might have a winemaker, a tasting room manager, a bookkeeper, and a handful of cellar and hospitality staff, with a harvest crew layered on top for eight weeks. If only half of them defer, a match costs you only what participants earn. It also rewards the people who save.

### The 3% nonelective is the predictable choice

If your cash flow swings with release dates, wine club shipments, and distributor payments, a flat 3% of eligible pay is easy to budget. It also reaches employees who never sign up to defer, which suits a younger tasting room team that tends not to enroll.

### QACA can lower the cost of turnover

A qualified automatic contribution arrangement enrolls employees by default and lets you apply a two-year vesting schedule to the employer contribution. If tasting room and cellar staff move on after a season or two, unvested dollars stay in the plan. The tradeoff is more administration and a more detailed notice. Ask your plan provider whether the added complexity pays for itself at your headcount.

## Who gets the notice, including seasonal and tasting room staff

The notice goes to every employee who is eligible for the plan, not only the ones who are already contributing. A plan can set eligibility at age 21 and one year of service, and that helps with true seasonal labor. A harvest worker who is with you for two months in a year generally will not meet a one-year-of-service requirement.

Part-time staff are a different story. The long-term part-time rules require plans to let employees defer once they have worked at least 500 hours in each of a set number of consecutive years. That number was three years for 2024 and drops to two years starting in 2025. A tasting room associate who works weekends and holidays every year can cross that line without anyone noticing. Ask your administrator to run the hours report before the notice goes out, so nobody in the eligible group is missed.

A few practical habits keep the notice clean:

- Deliver it by email with a read receipt or through your payroll portal, and keep proof of delivery.
- Send it early in November rather than the last week, so a bounce or a missed address can be fixed.
- Give new hires the notice by the time they become eligible, not at the next December cycle.
- Keep the dated copy with your plan records, since an auditor will ask for it.

If payroll runs through a [fixed-fee outsourced accounting arrangement](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting), the eligibility and hours data is already in one place. That makes the report much faster to pull.

## What safe harbor does to nondiscrimination testing

A regular 401(k) has to pass the actual deferral percentage (ADP) test, and any employer match has to pass the actual contribution percentage (ACP) test. These tests compare what highly compensated employees (HCEs) put in against what everyone else does. An owner with more than 5% of the business is always an HCE, and so are family members the ownership rules attribute to the owner.

Here is why that matters at a winery. Suppose your nonhighly compensated staff average a 1.5% deferral. Under the ADP rules, when that average is 2% or less, the HCE group can defer at most twice that, which is 3%. On a $150,000 W-2 salary, you could defer about $4,500 before the plan fails. Without safe harbor, the plan has to refund the excess to you, and that refund is taxable income in the year you receive it, which is the opposite of what you wanted.

A properly designed safe harbor plan skips the ADP test, and the match design can skip the ACP test as well. Most safe harbor plans are also exempt from the top-heavy minimum contribution, provided they only receive safe harbor contributions and deferrals. Owners can then put in up to the annual IRS dollar limit, which changes each year, without worrying about how the harvest crew chose to save.

Safe harbor does not remove every requirement. You still file the annual Form 5500, deposit deferrals on time, and follow the plan document. Anyone who tells you the plan is "testing free" has skipped some of the fine print.

## A Walla Walla example with real numbers

Here is an illustrative winery, not a specific client. It is an S corporation with 14 eligible employees. The owner-winemaker takes $150,000 in W-2 wages. The other 13 people earn $470,000 combined, so total eligible pay is $620,000.

| Design | How cost is calculated | Annual employer cost |
|---|---|---|
| 3% nonelective | 3% × $620,000 | $18,600 |
| Basic match (owner plus 6 employees at 4%+) | 4% × ($150,000 + 6 × $40,000) | $15,600 |
| Basic match (owner plus 2 employees at 4%+) | 4% × ($150,000 + 2 × $40,000) | $9,200 |

The nonelective costs more, but you know the number in January. The match costs less if participation stays low, and it floats with enrollment. A good tax plan also looks at what the owner gets back. In the nonelective case, $4,500 of that $18,600 goes to the owner's own account, and the owner can still defer to the full IRS limit. Depending on the structure, that is a deductible contribution to your own retirement that does not depend on anyone else's behavior.

Erin Denney, CPA, who leads tax planning for closely held businesses as Tax Manager at TK Partners, works on questions like this: how entity structure, owner compensation, and multi-year tax strategy shape a plan decision for owner-operators. A winery that is an S corporation, a partnership, or a sole proprietor has different compensation and deduction mechanics. The right design on paper can look different once those mechanics are applied.

## How employer contributions reach your tax return

Employer contributions are generally deductible for the year if you make them by the due date of the business return, including extensions. That gives you room to fund the nonelective after you know how the vintage and the year ended up. A match is usually deposited with each payroll, though some plans true it up annually, and your plan document controls which.

There are three timing points to plan for:

1. **Cash versus deduction.** A winery carries heavy barrel and bottle inventory, so cash can be tight in the first quarter even in a profitable year. A funding date of September 15 or October 15 on an extended return gives you room to catch up after the holiday season.
2. **The owner's deferral.** Owner deferrals have to come through payroll during the year. They cannot be added after December 31.
3. **Estimated taxes.** A deduction that exists on paper in October but arrives in April does not help the quarterly payment due in January. Your CPA should model the effect.

This is the kind of question [tax planning with a CPA](/what-we-do/income-tax) is built for. The goal is a number you can plan around, not a surprise on the March return.

## If you do not have a 401(k) yet

The cleanest start is a new plan effective January 1. In that case the notice is delivered by the time employees become eligible, and the plan needs to be adopted and set up with a provider before the year starts. Doing this in November leaves enough time to pick a recordkeeper, settle on a design, and set up payroll deductions before the first January paycheck.

For a winery, a few questions drive the choice:

- Do you want the plan mostly for your own savings, or as a benefit to keep a good cellar and hospitality team?
- Would a 3% nonelective contribution fit your cash flow, or would you prefer a match that depends on enrollment?
- Are you ready to take on the plan's ongoing administration, including the annual 5500 filing?

Owners with very few employees sometimes find a different plan type is a better fit, and that is worth a short conversation before committing. A CPA who knows your payroll and your books can narrow the options quickly. If you also have questions about entity type or system setup, those sit under [business foundation services](/what-we-do/business-foundation-services).

## A November checklist for winery owners

1. **Pull your plan document.** Confirm whether you are on a safe harbor match, a nonelective, or a regular plan.
2. **Confirm the plan year.** Calendar-year plans have the December 1 deadline. A fiscal-year plan has a different one.
3. **Run the eligibility report.** Include part-time and tasting room staff approaching the 500-hour threshold.
4. **Decide the design.** Compare the match and the 3% nonelective against your projected payroll and cash flow.
5. **Send the notice early, and keep proof of delivery.**
6. **Model the deduction.** Ask your CPA how the contribution lands on your return and your estimated payments.
7. **Talk to your plan administrator.** Make sure the amendment and notice match what you decided.

Winery accounting is seasonal, and it helps to have someone who understands that. A CPA who already knows your [winery's books](/wineries), vintage by vintage, can usually put the plan numbers together in a single sitting.

## Common Questions

**When is the safe harbor 401(k) notice deadline for a calendar-year plan?**

For a plan that runs January 1 to December 31, the notice has to reach eligible employees 30 to 90 days before the plan year starts, which makes the deadline about December 1. The window opens in early October. Plans using the 3% nonelective no longer need the annual notice.

**Does a safe harbor plan remove nondiscrimination testing for a winery?**

It removes the ADP test, and the ACP test too when the match is designed to qualify. Most safe harbor plans are also exempt from top-heavy minimums. You still file Form 5500, make deposits on time, and follow the plan document, so the plan is lighter on testing but not free of rules.

**Can I add a safe harbor design after the year has started?**

Sometimes. The SECURE Act lets a plan adopt the nonelective design late, up to 30 days before year-end for a 3% contribution, or later in the following year at 4%. A match does not get the same flexibility. Ask your administrator before making a promise to employees.

If the December 1 date is close and you are not sure which design fits your winery, [reach out to TK Partners](/contact). A CPA in Walla Walla or Moses Lake can look at your payroll, your plan document, and your tax picture with you, so the decision is made on time and with numbers you trust.

### How to turn a second home into a tax win
URL: /resources/how-to-turn-a-second-home-into-a-tax-win

After a Walla Walla harvest, the quiet stretch between December and February makes a cabin at Lake Chelan or a beach house on the Long Beach Peninsula look very appealing. A second home feels like a reward. Whether the IRS treats it as a reward or as a rental business comes down to a few day counts, and you control most of them.

That is good news. Handled with a plan, a second home can produce deductions, cover part of its own carrying costs, and still leave room for your own getaways. Here is how the second home tax rules work, with a winery owner's calendar in mind.

## The day count decides how the IRS sees your second home

The IRS sorts a vacation property into one of three buckets based on two numbers: how many days you rent it at a fair price, and how many days you use it personally. [IRS Publication 527](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p527) lays out the framework, and [Tax Topic 415](https://www.irs.gov/taxtopics/tc415) gives the short version.

The pivot is the so-called IRS 14 day rule for a second home. Your home counts as a personal residence if your personal use exceeds the greater of 14 days or 10% of the days you rent it at fair rental price. Cross that line and the tax treatment changes. Stay under it and the property is treated like a rental.

| Your situation | Tax treatment | What it means for you |
|---|---|---|
| Rented fewer than 15 days a year | Rental income is tax-free and not reported | No rental deductions, but mortgage interest and property taxes may still be itemized |
| Rented 15 or more days, personal use over the greater of 14 days or 10% of rental days | Mixed-use residence | Rental deductions are capped at rental income, so no tax loss |
| Rented 15 or more days, personal use at or under that threshold | Rental property | Full rental deductions and depreciation, though passive loss rules still apply |

A quick example of the 10% test: rent the home for 200 days and your threshold is 20 personal days, because 10% of 200 beats 14. Rent it for 90 days and the threshold stays at 14, because 10% of 90 is only 9.

## Which days count as personal use

More days count than most owners expect. A day is personal use if any of these people use the home:

- You or anyone who owns a share of it
- Your family members, even if they pay rent
- Anyone using it under a home swap arrangement
- Anyone paying less than a fair rental price

So the week your brother-in-law spends there at a friends-and-family rate is a personal day. So is the weekend you lend it to a distributor for free. Days you spend working on repairs and maintenance for most of the day do not count as personal use, even if family tags along. That matters in spring, when a property needs a deep clean and a deck refinish before the rental season.

## The under-15-day rental: the quietest tax perk

If you rent the home for fewer than 15 days in a year, you do not report the income. At all. Tax Topic 415 spells this out, and it is one of the few places the tax code simply lets you keep money.

This suits a property near a big event, like a lake house during a summer festival weekend, or a Walla Walla home rented out for a single release weekend when rooms in town are scarce. Rent it for 10 days at $500 a night and the $5,000 stays out of your return.

The tradeoff is that you cannot deduct rental expenses. Mortgage interest and property taxes are still itemized deductions if you itemize, subject to the usual limits, including the cap on state and local taxes and the limit on mortgage debt. Washington has no state income tax, so the cap is one more reason many owners here find the standard deduction wins anyway.

## The mixed-use home: income without a loss

Say you want to rent more often and also use the home yourself for three weeks. You land in the middle bucket. The home is treated as a residence, and rental income is fully taxable.

Expenses get split by days. Rental-day expenses are deducted in a set order: mortgage interest and property taxes first, then operating costs like utilities, cleaning, and insurance, then depreciation last. The deductions cannot push you below zero. Whatever you cannot use carries forward to a future year when the home earns more.

This is the bucket where owners get surprised. They book a few extra family weeks, expecting a deduction, and discover depreciation has been squeezed out entirely.

## The rental-property route and what it takes

Keep personal use at or under the threshold and the property is a rental. Now every allocable expense counts, including depreciation over 27.5 years on the building (land does not depreciate). Depreciation is a deduction with no cash attached, which is why a property can put money in your pocket and still show a tax loss.

A worked example, simplified for illustration. Suppose a Lake Chelan house is rented 80 nights at $325, which is $26,000 of income. You use it 12 days yourself, under the 14-day threshold. Annual costs are $14,000 in mortgage interest, $4,500 in property tax, $2,200 in insurance, and $5,000 in utilities and cleaning, plus about $14,500 of depreciation on a $400,000 building.

Rental days are 80 of 92 total days used, about 87%. That makes roughly $22,350 of the cash costs and $12,650 of the depreciation allocable to the rental. Cash flow is positive by about $3,650 after those costs. On paper, the property shows a loss near $9,000.

Now change one thing. Use the home 20 days instead of 12. You crossed the threshold, and rental days are 80 of 100. Interest and taxes allocable to rental come to about $14,800, and operating costs to about $5,760. That leaves only about $5,440 of income to absorb depreciation, and the rest carries forward. Eight extra days of personal use cost you the ability to produce a loss at all.

Your actual allocation depends on the facts of your property, so treat these figures as a model, not a promise.

## Why a winery owner's income changes the math

Here is where winery owners differ from the typical buyer. Rental losses are generally passive. Passive losses can offset passive income, not the profits from the winery you actively run. There is a special allowance of up to $25,000 for rental losses when you actively participate, but it phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of modified adjusted gross income. Many winery owners earn above that, so the paper loss gets suspended rather than deducted.

Suspended is not lost. The loss carries forward, offsets future rental income, and is released when you sell the property. Still, if you buy expecting a big deduction this year, you may be disappointed. Buying for cash flow and long-term appreciation, with the depreciation as a bonus, is a sounder footing.

A few winery-specific planning points:

- **Crush shapes your calendar.** August through October is when you can least use the property and when it rents best in many vacation areas. Block your personal days for the quiet months and count them carefully.
- **Keep the house out of the winery entity.** Mixing a personal-use property into your tasting room's LLC can muddy both sets of books and complicate any later sale. Multi-year entity questions like this are what Erin Denney, CPA, and our tax team work through with owner-operators.
- **Rental of under 30 days has local tax rules.** Short stays in Washington generally carry sales tax and local lodging tax, and cities and counties set their own short-term rental permits. Check before your first booking.
- **Selling is a separate tax event.** A second home does not qualify for the home sale exclusion unless it was your main home for two of the last five years, and depreciation you claimed is taxed when you sell, at up to 25%.

## Second home vs investment property

The choice between a second home and an investment property is mostly a question of how you behave once you own it. A true second home leans personal: you use it often, rent it rarely, and treat the tax side as secondary. An investment property leans on rental income, with personal use capped around two weeks.

Both can be a sound purchase. The mistake is buying an investment property and then living in it half the summer, or buying a second home and budgeting as if rental income were guaranteed. Decide which one you are buying before you close, and write the plan down. If you are still weighing whether to buy at all, our walkthrough on [the math behind renting vs. buying a home](/resources/do-the-math-behind-renting-vs-buying-a-home) is a good place to pressure-test the monthly cost.

## Records that keep your position safe

The day count is only as good as your proof. Keep a simple calendar, shared with your property manager, that marks every night as one of three types: rented at fair price, personal use, or repairs and maintenance. Save booking platform reports, cleaning invoices, and the closing statement showing your purchase price and land value. If the IRS asks, the calendar does the talking.

This is a natural fit for the year-round work in our [income tax planning](/what-we-do/income-tax). A midyear check on the day count in July tells you whether to rent more or use the house less in the fall, while there is still time to change the outcome.

## Common Questions

**What is the IRS 14 day rule for a second home?**

If you rent a home for fewer than 15 days a year, the income is tax-free and unreported. Separately, personal use above the greater of 14 days or 10% of rental days makes the home a residence, which limits rental deductions to rental income.

**Is vacation home rental income taxable?**

Yes, if you rent the property for 15 or more days. You report the income and deduct allocable expenses on Schedule E. If the home is a mixed-use residence, deductions cannot exceed income, so the rental will not generate a loss.

**Can I deduct my second home mortgage interest?**

Often, yes. Interest on a second home is generally deductible as an itemized deduction, within the mortgage debt limit. If you rent the home out enough, the rental portion is deducted against rental income instead, following the allocation rules.

## Plan the days before you buy the house

A second home is easiest to get right before you close, when the numbers are still flexible. If you are a winery owner in Walla Walla weighing a purchase, [contact TK Partners](/contact) and bring your draft calendar and the property's expected rents. A CPA on our team will model the day counts with you, so the house you buy is the tax outcome you meant to buy. If your winery's own books also need a careful eye, our [winery accounting services](/wineries) are built for exactly that.

### Your time is priceless, but the IRS won't deduct it: volunteer tax deductions for Walla Walla wineries
URL: /resources/your-time-is-priceless-but-the-irs-wont-deduct-it-what-you-c

Last harvest, you probably gave a Saturday to a good cause. Maybe you poured at a school fundraiser, hauled tables for a charity auction, or sat through a long board meeting for a local nonprofit. Then tax season arrived and a fair question surfaced: does any of that count? The honest answer has two halves. The hours themselves are never deductible. But the money you spent to volunteer often is, as long as you know the rules and keep the right records.

## Why the IRS won't deduct your time

The IRS treats a charitable deduction as a gift of money or property. Your labor is neither. If you spend 40 hours organizing a fundraiser and your usual rate is $150 an hour, that is $6,000 of value you gave away, and $0 you can deduct. [IRS Publication 526](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p526) says it plainly: you cannot deduct the value of your time or services.

There is a logic to it. You never reported that $6,000 as income, so there is nothing to offset. It still stings for owner-operators, whose time is often the scarcest resource in the business. During crush, an afternoon away from the cellar has a real cost. The tax code just doesn't count it.

The other half of the misconception is the opposite mistake: assuming that because the time is out, everything else is too. It isn't.

## The out-of-pocket costs that can be deducted

Unreimbursed expenses that are directly connected to your volunteer work for a qualified organization can be deductible. "Directly connected" and "unreimbursed" are the two phrases doing the heavy lifting. Here is how common situations sort out.

| Expense | Deductible? | What to know |
|---|---|---|
| Driving to and from volunteer work | Yes | 14 cents per mile, or actual gas and oil costs |
| Parking and tolls | Yes | Keep the receipt or a note of the date and place |
| Supplies you buy for the event | Yes | Name tags, signage, serving supplies, ingredients |
| Meals and lodging on an overnight trip as a volunteer | Yes, if no significant personal pleasure or vacation element | Must be away from home overnight |
| Uniform required by the charity and not suited to everyday wear | Yes | A logo T-shirt you could wear to dinner does not qualify |
| The value of your time | No | Never deductible |
| Childcare while you volunteer | No | Not a charitable expense |
| Car insurance, depreciation, general repairs | No | Only gas and oil, or the mileage rate |
| Anything the charity paid back to you | No | You can only deduct what you absorbed |

The charitable mileage deduction is the one that surprises people, because the rate is low. It is set by statute at 14 cents per mile, not by the IRS each year like the business rate. Picture a Walla Walla tasting room owner who serves on the board of a nonprofit in Milton-Freewater. She drives a 22-mile round trip to 30 meetings and events in a year. That is 660 miles, or $92.40 of deduction. Real, but modest.

Here is a wrinkle worth knowing. If you keep records of your actual gas and oil costs, you can deduct those instead of the flat rate. At 20 miles per gallon and $4 gas, you spend about 20 cents a mile on fuel, so the actual-cost method can win. You choose one method per year for the volunteer driving, not a mix of both.

## You have to itemize for any of it to matter

Here is the catch that quietly ends most of these conversations. Volunteer expenses are charitable contributions, and charitable contributions are claimed on Schedule A. That only helps if your itemized deductions exceed the standard deduction. For 2025, the standard deduction is $15,750 for a single filer and $31,500 for married couples filing jointly.

A $92 mileage deduction will not move the needle if you are nowhere near those numbers. It can matter if you are already itemizing because of a mortgage, property taxes, large cash gifts, or medical costs. Washington has no state income tax on wages, so there is no state return to pull you toward itemizing either. The decision is purely federal.

This is also why bunching can make sense. If you give generously every year but fall just short of the threshold, concentrating two years of giving into one can push you over. Then you take the standard deduction in the off year. Your [tax planning](/what-we-do/income-tax) is the place to model that, using your real numbers instead of a guess.

## Where winery owners tend to get tripped up

Wine country has its own version of charitable life. Benefit dinners, barrel auctions, charity pours, and scholarship events fill the Walla Walla calendar, and each has a tax wrinkle.

**Benefit tickets and auction purchases.** If you pay $250 for a dinner with wine pairings that is worth $90, only the $160 above fair market value is a gift. When you pay more than $75 and receive something in return, the charity must give you a written disclosure of that value. The same logic applies to auction items. You deduct the excess over what the item is worth, not the whole bid.

**Donating your own wine.** Pouring at an event is volunteering. Handing over cases for the silent auction is a contribution of inventory. For most owners, the deduction is generally your cost, not the $38 shelf price on a bottle that costs you $14 to produce. The cost also has to come out of cost of goods sold so it is not deducted twice. Getting this wrong is a common reason an otherwise generous year turns into a messy return. Our [winery accounting team](/wineries) tracks inventory by vintage, which makes this a clean adjustment instead of a scramble.

**Sponsorships.** If you sponsor an event and get your logo on the banner, the IRS may see advertising, not a gift. Advertising can be a deductible business expense, but it belongs on a different line of the return. Which line depends on what you received in exchange.

**Mixing business and volunteering.** If you pour your wines at a charity event and also meet distributors, the trip may be partly business. Mileage for the business portion belongs in your business records. Mileage for the volunteer portion belongs on Schedule A. Do not claim the same miles twice. Getting the split right is the kind of line-drawing we do in our [tax work](/what-we-do/income-tax). It is similar in spirit to sorting out whether a vineyard dog is a [business deduction or a pet](/resources/unless-its-working-for-you-your-dog-isnt-a-tax-deduction).

## The qualified organization test

The deduction only works if the group is a qualified organization. Most 501(c)(3) charities, schools, churches, and certain government units qualify. Social clubs, civic leagues, and individuals do not, and neither does a crowdfunding page for a neighbor. Before you spend money, you can look the group up in the IRS Tax Exempt Organization Search, which is part of the [IRS Charities and Nonprofits hub](https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits). It takes two minutes and prevents a disallowed deduction.

## The records that hold up

The IRS does not need you to be perfect. It needs you to be contemporaneous. A few habits cover almost everything:

- **Mileage log.** Date, destination, the charity, and miles driven. A notes app works as well as a paper notebook.
- **Receipts for supplies, parking, and travel.** Photograph them the day you buy them.
- **A statement from the charity if your unreimbursed expenses reach $250.** It should describe the services you provided, give the date, and say whether the charity gave you anything in return.
- **A note of what was reimbursed.** If the charity repays part of your costs, only the remainder counts.

None of that is hard. It just has to happen in the moment, not in February when you cannot remember if the third Thursday was the school auction or the board retreat.

## A simple way to decide what is worth tracking

Track everything during the year, since it costs you almost nothing. Then, before filing, ask three questions. Will I itemize? Do my volunteer expenses add up to anything meaningful alongside my cash gifts and any donated wine? And did anyone reimburse me? Your CPA can answer the first question in minutes with your numbers in front of them. The records you kept make the other two easy.

## Common Questions

**Can I deduct the hours I spend volunteering?**

No. The IRS does not allow a deduction for the value of your time or services, whatever your hourly rate. You can deduct unreimbursed, directly connected costs like mileage, parking, supplies, and qualifying travel, provided you itemize deductions and the organization is a qualified charity.

**How much is the charitable mileage deduction?**

The rate is 14 cents per mile for driving in service of a qualified charity. You can instead deduct actual gas and oil costs, which can be higher when fuel prices are up. Either way, keep a log with the date, destination, purpose, and miles for each trip.

**Do I need a receipt from the charity for volunteer expenses?**

If your unreimbursed expenses for one organization total $250 or more, you need a written statement from the charity describing your services, the date, and whether it gave you anything in return. You also need your own records, such as a mileage log and receipts, to support each cost.

## Talk it through before you file

Volunteering should feel like giving, not like an audit risk. If you want help sorting out what counts, how to handle donated wine or sponsorships, and whether itemizing makes sense this year, [reach out to our team](/contact). We will go through your giving in plain language and make sure your good deeds are documented well enough to hold up.
